set1.q: A 69-year-old man has sudden severe pain in his right leg. Pulses are absent below the knee. Which examination finding is often the earliest neurologic sign of acute vascular insufficiency?
opts: Sensory loss over the foot's dorsum
Correct. Light-touch sensory fibers are highly susceptible to ischemia, so sensory deficits over the dorsum of the foot are often the earliest neurologic sign of acute vascular insufficiency.
Complete paralysis of the leg
Profound paralysis marks an irreversibly ischemic limb, a late finding. Sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot appears earlier because light-touch fibers are most sensitive.
Absent patellar reflex
Reflex testing is not named as the early sign. Light-touch sensory fibers fail first, so loss of sensation over the dorsum of the foot comes earliest.
Loss of hair on the shin
Hair loss is a chronic peripheral artery disease finding from long-standing poor flow. In acute ischemia the earliest neurologic sign is dorsal foot sensory loss.

set1.q: A 68-year-old man has a 3.1 cm femoral pseudoaneurysm that has persisted since his catheterization. Which treatment seals the leak?
opts: Catheter-directed thrombolysis
Thrombolysis is for acute arterial thrombus under 14 days. A pseudoaneurysm is sealed by promoting clot, with ultrasound-guided thrombin.
Ultrasound-guided thrombin injection
Correct. Treatment of a pseudoaneurysm that does not regress is ultrasound-guided injection of thrombin, which promotes clotting and seals the leak.
Watch and wait
Watchful waiting is for pseudoaneurysms under 2 cm, which may thrombose on their own. A persistent 3.1 cm cavity needs thrombin injection.
Intravenous heparin
Heparin prevents the clotting that seals the cavity. The leak is sealed by ultrasound-guided thrombin injection.

Amputation is for irreversible limbs with profound sensory loss, paralysis and absent venous signals. This limb is still salvageable with immediate revascularization.
In the surgical suite, without delay
Correct. An immediately threatened limb is salvageable only with immediate revascularization, so it should preferentially undergo further evaluation and treatment in a surgical suite.
After outpatient duplex imaging
Outpatient testing wastes the time this limb does not have. Sensory loss beyond the toes with weakness means immediate revascularization in a surgical suite.
After computed tomography first

Catheter-directed thrombolysis

Ultrasound-guided thrombin

Carotid endarterectomy

set1.q: A 66-year-old woman with a 4.8 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm has a history of severe reaction to contrast dye. She is stable, and the extent of the aneurysm must be defined. Which imaging is most appropriate?
opts: Conventional angiography
Conventional angiography needs contrast injection into the artery. For a stable patient with dye allergy, magnetic resonance imaging is the alternative.
Magnetic resonance imaging
Correct. Magnetic resonance imaging is comparable to computed tomography without exposure to dye or ionizing radiation, which makes it useful in stable patients with a dye allergy.
Computed tomography angiography
Computed tomography angiography relies on contrast dye, which her allergy precludes. Magnetic resonance imaging gives comparable detail without dye.
Abdominal X-ray
A plain film shows only a calcified outline, and misses a quarter of aneurysms. It cannot define extent; magnetic resonance imaging can, without dye.

set1.q: A 63-year-old man has an incidental 4.0 cm ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm on a chest radiograph and follow-up imaging. He has no symptoms. Which surveillance plan is appropriate?
opts: Abdominal ultrasound every three years with no other imaging
Three-yearly ultrasound is the plan for small abdominal aneurysms and cannot see the thoracic aorta. His surveillance is computed tomography or magnetic resonance.
Open repair with aortic root replacement within the month
Asymptomatic ascending repair is generally indicated above 5.5 cm or with growth over 0.5 cm per year. At 4.0 cm he needs surveillance, not surgery.
Computed tomography or magnetic resonance every 3 to 5 years
Correct. Thoracic aneurysms under 4.5 cm are followed with computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging every three to five years; 4.5 to 5.4 cm moves to every six to 12 months.
Computed tomography or magnetic resonance every 6 to 12 months
Six-to-12-monthly imaging applies to thoracic aneurysms of 4.5 to 5.4 cm. At 4.0 cm the interval is every three to five years.

set1.q: A 70-year-old man with hypertension reports calf pain after walking about two blocks that resolves with rest. His ankle-brachial index is 0.62 on the left and normal on the right. Which interpretation fits the left-sided value?
opts: Rest pain and tissue loss range
Rest pain, ulcers and gangrene sit in the 0 to 0.4 band, the critical limb ischemia range. A value of 0.62 is higher, in the claudication band.
Noncompressible artery range
A falsely high reading above 1.3 signals calcified, noncompressible arteries, as in diabetes. A value of 0.62 is genuinely reduced and lies in the claudication band.
Claudication range
Correct. An ankle-brachial index between 0.4 and 0.9 is the claudication band, matching exertional calf pain relieved by rest. The lower of the two legs is taken as the overall index.
Normal range
A normal ankle-brachial index lies above 0.9 up to 1.3. A value of 0.62 is reduced and falls in the claudication band of 0.4 to 0.9.

set1.q: A 68-year-old man has had a cold, pulseless right leg for three hours, with pallor, tingling and mild weakness of the toes. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Immediate vascular surgery consult

Correct. Acute limb ischemia is a vascular emergency; management begins with an immediate vascular surgery consult, anticoagulation with intravenous heparin, and testing chosen by the category of ischemia.
Outpatient ankle-brachial index
The ankle-brachial index is the initial test for chronic peripheral artery disease. A sudden pulseless leg needs an immediate vascular surgery consult, not clinic testing.
Supervised exercise referral
Exercise therapy improves walking distance in stable claudication. A cold, pulseless, weak leg is an acute occlusion needing an immediate vascular surgery consult.
Start cilostazol and follow up
Cilostazol is an oral antiplatelet for chronic claudication. An acute occlusion with sensory and motor change needs an immediate vascular surgery consult.

set1.q: A 58-year-old man who smokes a pack a day has calf claudication and an ankle-brachial index of 0.7. He asks what matters most for his legs. Which counseling point is most important?
opts: Stop smoking completely

Correct. Cigarette smoking triples the risk of peripheral artery disease compared with nonsmokers, and smoking cessation heads the list of risk-factor reduction measures for every patient with the disease.
Limit walking to avoid pain
Consistent moderate exercise improves walking distance, so avoiding walking works against him. Exercise therapy, at least 30 to 45 minutes three times a week, is part of management.
Elevate the legs when painful
Elevation removes gravity's help to arterial flow and worsens ischemic pain. The priority for this smoker is complete smoking cessation, which heads risk-factor reduction.
Switch to occasional cigars
Any continued tobacco use keeps driving atherosclerosis; smoking triples the risk of peripheral artery disease. The counseling goal is complete cessation, not a change of product.

set1.q: A 69-year-old man has pain in both legs when walking, with numbness and weakness. Standing still does not help; the pain eases only when he sits down or leans forward over a shopping cart. His pedal pulses are normal. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Spinal stenosis

Correct. Spinal stenosis gives claudication-like symptoms with numbness and weakness, relieved by rest and also by sitting down or leaning forward to straighten the lumbar spine. Normal pulses argue against arterial disease.
Peripheral artery disease
Arterial claudication is relieved by rest alone, usually within 10 minutes, and brings diminished pulses below the stenosis. Needing to sit or lean forward points to spinal stenosis.
Peripheral neuropathy
Peripheral neuropathy causes continuous burning in the feet that is unaffected by exercise. His pain is triggered by walking and relieved by sitting or leaning forward.
Venous insufficiency
Venous insufficiency causes calf swelling and discomfort with standing, worse with prolonged walking. Numbness, weakness and relief with forward flexion fit spinal stenosis.

set1.q: A 66-year-old man with hypertension has sudden, severe, ripping chest pain. His electrocardiogram is normal. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Computed tomography, chest and abdomen
Correct. The electrocardiogram may be normal in aortic dissection, so a normal tracing does not exclude it; computed tomography of the chest and abdomen delineates the extent of the dissection.
Reassure him; the tracing is normal
A normal electrocardiogram is common in aortic dissection and does not rule it out. Sudden tearing pain needs computed tomography of the chest and abdomen.
Ankle-brachial index measurement
The ankle-brachial index grades leg arterial disease. Suspected dissection is imaged with computed tomography of the chest and abdomen.
Abdominal plain radiograph
A plain film cannot show an intimal tear or false lumen. Computed tomography of the chest and abdomen delineates the extent.

set1.q: A 68-year-old man who smokes and has diabetes reports aching in both buttocks and hips after walking two blocks, relieved by about 10 minutes of rest. He also reports erectile dysfunction. Both femoral pulses are diminished. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Tibial artery disease
Tibial and peroneal disease produces foot claudication with normal femoral pulses. Buttock pain, erectile dysfunction and weak femoral pulses point to the aortoiliac segment.
Aortoiliac occlusive disease

Correct. Buttock and hip claudication points to the aortoiliac segment, and the triad of claudication, absent or diminished femoral pulses and erectile dysfunction is Leriche syndrome, the severe form of aortoiliac disease.
Superficial femoral artery disease
Superficial femoral stenosis gives upper two-thirds calf claudication, the most common site. Buttock and hip pain with weak femoral pulses places the lesion higher, in the aortoiliac segment.
Lumbar spinal stenosis
Spinal stenosis mimics claudication but brings numbness and weakness and is relieved only by sitting or leaning forward. It does not diminish the femoral pulses or cause this triad.

set1.q: A 70-year-old man presents with painful blue toes and palpable pedal pulses. On abdominal examination there is a pulsatile mass above the umbilicus. Which lesion is the likely source of his emboli?
opts: Carotid artery plaque
Carotid plaque embolizes to the brain and retina, causing transient ischemic attack or stroke. Emboli to the toes with a pulsatile abdominal mass come from the aorta.
Femoral pseudoaneurysm
A femoral pseudoaneurysm follows catheterization and causes local pain from swelling. A pulsatile abdominal mass with blue toes indicates an abdominal aortic aneurysm.
Thoracic aortic dissection
Dissection presents with sudden tearing chest pain from an intimal tear. The pulsatile abdominal mass here is an abdominal aortic aneurysm shedding emboli to the toes.
Abdominal aortic aneurysm
Correct. Atheroemboli originate from proximal atherosclerotic plaques, and an abdominal aortic aneurysm can itself shed emboli, producing blue toe syndrome as one of its embolic phenomena.

opts: Computed tomography angiography
Correct. Viable and marginally threatened limbs, with no sensory loss or weakness, allow sufficient time for vascular imaging such as computed tomography angiography before treatment.
Immediate major amputation
Amputation is for irreversibly ischemic limbs with profound sensory loss and paralysis. Her limb has no neurologic deficit and there is time to image it.
Direct transfer to the surgical suite
Immediately threatened limbs, with sensory loss beyond the toes and weakness, go straight to the surgical suite. With no deficit there is time for imaging first.
Discharge with oral aspirin

set1.q: A 68-year-old man with a 5.9 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm is being prepared for repair. Which study is best for diagnosis and pre-intervention planning?
opts: Abdominal X-ray
A plain film may show a calcified outline in about 75% of aneurysms but cannot define extent for planning. Computed tomography angiography does.
Transesophageal echocardiography
Transesophageal echocardiography evaluates the aortic valve and aortic root in thoracic disease. Abdominal repair is planned with computed tomography angiography.
Computed tomography angiography
Correct. Computed tomography angiography is the best diagnostic and pre-intervention planning study, accurately delineating the aneurysm's location, size and extent.
Abdominal ultrasound
Ultrasound is the study of choice for initial screening and serial size measurement. It is not the best study for planning repair.

set1.q: A 72-year-old man with extensive atherosclerosis develops painful, tender, bluish discoloration of several toes on his left foot, with localized pallor. His dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are easily palpable. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Acute embolic limb ischemia
A thromboembolus occluding a limb artery produces a cold, pale leg with absent pulses. Palpable pulses with painful blue toes point to atheroembolism.
Critical limb ischemia
Critical limb ischemia is chronic rest pain and tissue loss with diminished pulses. Sudden painful blue toes with easily palpable pulses is atheroembolism.
Dry gangrene
Dry gangrene is hard, black, mummified tissue with clear demarcation. Tender blue toes with palpable pulses reflect small-vessel atheroemboli.
Atheroembolism

Correct. Atheroemboli of fibrin, platelets and cholesterol debris from proximal plaques lodge in small vessels of muscle and skin, causing blue toe syndrome with tenderness and pallor while distal pulses usually stay palpable.

set1.q: A 70-year-old man has constant hypogastric and low back pain for two days. A tender pulsatile mass is felt; blood pressure is 152/90 and stable. Imaging shows a 5.8 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm without rupture. Which management is most appropriate?
opts: Discharge with smoking advice
Smoking cessation is part of long-term care, but a painful, expanding aneurysm cannot be sent home. It needs blood pressure control and repair.
Refer once it reaches 6.5 cm
Aneurysmal pain warrants urgent referral regardless of size, and this one already exceeds the repair threshold. Beta blockade and repair are indicated.
Beta blocker and surgical repair

Correct. A symptomatic unruptured aneurysm needs assessment of stability, large-bore intravenous access, pain control, blood pressure control with beta blockers, and surgical repair unless contraindicated.
Ultrasound again in six months
Surveillance is for asymptomatic aneurysms. Pain from aneurysmal expansion means he needs blood pressure control and surgical repair now.

set1.q: A 76-year-old woman has constant throbbing, burning pain in her toes and forefoot that is worse lying flat, not relieved by narcotic pain medicine, and eased by dangling her leg or walking around. Her feet are cool. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Peripheral neuropathy
Neuropathic burning is continuous and unaffected by exercise or position. Pain relieved by dependency and worse on elevation is arterial rest pain.
Acute limb ischemia
Acute limb ischemia is a sudden occlusion with abrupt severe pain and absent pulses. Her pain is long-standing and position-dependent, the pattern of critical limb ischemia.
Critical limb ischemia

Correct. Ischemic rest pain of critical limb ischemia is constant, distal, worse with elevation or reclining, poorly controlled even by narcotics, and relieved by dependency or walking, which use gravity to aid perfusion.
Intermittent claudication
Claudication is pain with activity relieved by rest, usually in about 10 minutes. Constant pain relieved by walking or dangling is ischemic rest pain.

set1.q: A 64-year-old woman with hypertension has a carotid bruit found on routine examination. She has never had neurologic symptoms. Duplex shows 35% stenosis. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Digital subtraction angiography
Digital subtraction angiography is used to guide interventions, and none is indicated here. Low-grade stenosis under 50% is managed medically.
Medical management

Correct. Medical management is advised for symptomatic and asymptomatic patients with low-grade stenosis under 50%: antiplatelet therapy, control of hypertension, diabetes and lipids, smoking cessation, diet, exercise and weight reduction.
Carotid endarterectomy
Endarterectomy is reserved for symptomatic stenosis over 70% or asymptomatic stenosis over 80% with a life expectancy over five years. A 35% stenosis is managed medically.
Carotid stenting
Stenting is an alternative revascularization for poor surgical candidates who meet surgical thresholds. A 35% asymptomatic stenosis needs medical management.

Pentoxifylline
Pentoxifylline is a xanthine derivative for chronic claudication. Acute arterial occlusion needs intravenous heparin anticoagulation and a vascular surgery consult.
Intravenous heparin
Correct. The medical therapy for acute peripheral arterial occlusion is anticoagulation with intravenous heparin, started alongside an immediate vascular surgery consult.

Aspirin is an antiplatelet agent for chronic peripheral artery disease. The medical therapy for an acute arterial occlusion is anticoagulation with intravenous heparin.

opts: Retroperitoneal rupture of the aorta
Retroperitoneal bleeding is the picture of a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm with shock. Her local pain comes from swelling and nerve compression.
Critical limb ischemia rest pain
Ischemic rest pain is forefoot pain relieved by dependency in chronic disease. Groin-to-thigh pain here reflects swelling and nerve compression.
Atheroemboli to the toes
Atheroemboli cause painful blue toes, not pain around a groin swelling. Pseudoaneurysm pain is from swelling pressure or nerve compression.
Swelling and nerve compression
Correct. A pseudoaneurysm presents with pain from increased pressure due to swelling or from nerve compression by the expanding blood-filled cavity.

opts: Asymptomatic carotid artery disease
Asymptomatic disease means stenosis with no stroke or transient ischemic attack in the last six months. His transient monocular vision loss makes him symptomatic.
Thoracic aortic aneurysm
Thoracic aneurysms are usually silent or cause regurgitation, hoarseness or compression symptoms. Transient monocular vision loss with a carotid bruit is carotid disease.
Aortic dissection
Dissection presents with sudden tearing chest pain. A brief curtain of vision loss in one eye with a carotid bruit points to symptomatic carotid disease.

Correct. Transient monocular blindness from interrupted retinal blood flow is a focal neurologic symptom; with a carotid bruit it classifies him as having symptomatic atherosclerotic carotid artery disease.

opts: Aortic regurgitation
Correct. Aortic dissection can cause aortic regurgitation through dilatation of the aortic root, producing a diastolic murmur and breathlessness.
Mitral stenosis
Mitral stenosis is not a listed consequence of dissection. Root dilatation in dissection causes aortic regurgitation.
Pseudoaneurysm
A pseudoaneurysm follows arterial puncture and causes local swelling and pain. The new diastolic murmur here is aortic regurgitation from root dilatation.
Carotid stenosis
Carotid stenosis is an atherosclerotic narrowing that produces neurologic symptoms, not a diastolic murmur. Root dilatation causes aortic regurgitation.

set1.q: A 66-year-old man with claudication and an ankle-brachial index of 0.72 has no bleeding history. Which medication class should be started to lower his risk of myocardial infarction and stroke?
opts: Intravenous heparin
Intravenous heparin is the medical therapy for acute peripheral arterial occlusion. Chronic claudication calls for an oral antiplatelet agent instead.
A loop diuretic
Diuretics treat fluid overload and have no role in claudication. Antiplatelet agents reduce myocardial infarction and stroke risk and improve walking distance.
An antiplatelet agent

Correct. Antiplatelet therapy (aspirin, clopidogrel or cilostazol) decreases the overall risk of cardiovascular disease from myocardial infarction and stroke and improves walking distance in peripheral artery disease.
A thrombolytic agent
Thrombolysis, such as catheter-directed alteplase, belongs to acute limb ischemia of under 14 days. Stable claudication is treated with an antiplatelet agent.

opts: Routine imaging in six months
Scheduled surveillance is for asymptomatic aneurysms. New chest or back pain requires urgent imaging to rule out the aneurysm as the cause.
Reassurance and pain relief
Treating pain without imaging risks missing an expanding or leaking aneurysm. Urgent imaging is required first.
Ankle-brachial index today
The ankle-brachial index assesses leg arteries and cannot explain chest pain. Urgent aortic imaging is required.
Urgent imaging of the aorta
Correct. Chest or back pain with a known or suspected thoracic aortic aneurysm must undergo urgent imaging to rule out the aneurysm as the cause of the pain.

set1.q: A 70-year-old man who had a large anterior myocardial infarction three weeks ago develops sudden pain and coldness of his right leg with absent foot pulses. Which cardiac finding is the most likely embolic source?
opts: A calcified mitral leaflet
Valve calcification is not the named cardiac source. After a myocardial infarction, a left ventricular thrombus is the classic origin of an embolus to the leg.
A pericardial effusion
Fluid around the heart does not form emboli. The cardiac sources named for limb emboli are atrial fibrillation and left ventricular thrombus after infarction.
An atrial septal scar
A septal scar is not a recognized embolic source here. Following myocardial infarction, a left ventricular thrombus can dislodge and occlude a smaller distal artery.
Left ventricular thrombus

Correct. Thromboemboli are the most common emboli, and the heart is the source in 80 to 90% of cases; a left ventricular thrombus after myocardial infarction is a named example, as is atrial fibrillation.

opts: Smoking harms only the leg arteries
Smoking drives atherosclerosis throughout the body and nearly doubles stroke risk. Cessation is central to managing carotid disease.
Smoking nearly doubles stroke risk

Correct. Smoking cessation is part of medical management of carotid disease because smoking nearly doubles the risk of stroke; it sits alongside antiplatelet therapy, comorbidity control, diet, exercise and weight reduction.
Aspirin cancels the smoking risk
Antiplatelet therapy does not neutralize tobacco. Smoking nearly doubles stroke risk, so cessation remains a core part of carotid disease management.
Quitting only matters before surgery
Smoking cessation is part of medical management for every patient with carotid disease, surgical or not, because smoking nearly doubles stroke risk.

set1.q: A 69-year-old woman with claudication, a known contrast allergy and reduced renal function needs arterial imaging before a planned intervention. Which study should be avoided?
opts: Ankle-brachial index
The ankle-brachial index is a simple bedside cuff test with no contrast at all. It is the important initial test and carries no risk for her kidneys.
Computed tomography angiography
Correct. Computed tomography angiography uses contrast to show arterial anatomy, and its contraindications are contrast allergy and decreased renal function, both of which she has.
Magnetic resonance angiography
Magnetic resonance angiography is the alternative for patients with contrast allergy. Its contraindications are pacemakers and intracranial aneurysm clips, which she does not have.
Duplex ultrasound
Duplex ultrasound is noninvasive and uses no contrast media or radiation, so it is safe here. It is the mainstay initial imaging when stenosis is suspected.

set1.q: A 75-year-old man with peripheral artery disease has a hard, dry, black distal toe with a clear line between healthy and dead tissue. There is no swelling, moisture or fever. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Atheroembolism
Atheroembolism causes painful blue toes with palpable pulses from cholesterol debris. A hard, black, mummified toe with clear demarcation is dry gangrene.
Dry gangrene
Correct. Dry gangrene has a hard, dry texture, usually involves the distal toes, shows clear demarcation between healthy and necrotic tissue, and is common in patients with peripheral artery disease.
Wet gangrene
Wet gangrene is moist and edematous with blistering and bacterial infection, and is a surgical emergency. This toe is hard, dry and clearly demarcated.
Gas gangrene
Gas gangrene is a wet gangrene from spore-forming clostridial species releasing toxins and gas. A dry, demarcated toe without fever is dry gangrene.

opts: Digital subtraction angiography
Digital subtraction angiography is the invasive gold standard, not used for screening; it guides therapeutic interventions. The initial carotid test is duplex ultrasonography.
Computed tomography of the chest
Chest computed tomography does not image the cervical carotid arteries. The most widely used initial carotid test is duplex ultrasonography.
Ankle-brachial index
The ankle-brachial index is the initial test for peripheral artery disease in the legs. Carotid stenosis is first assessed with duplex ultrasonography.
Duplex ultrasonography
Correct. Duplex ultrasonography is the most widely used initial screening tool for carotid stenosis and is also used to monitor patients serially for progression or after intervention.

set2.q: A 70-year-old man with a recent transient ischemic attack has a high-grade carotid stenosis on duplex and is being prepared for intervention. Which study is considered the gold standard?
opts: Magnetic resonance angiography
Magnetic resonance angiography images the cervical and intracranial circulation and brain very effectively. The gold standard, however, is digital subtraction angiography.
Carotid auscultation for a bruit
A bruit is an examination finding, auscultated one side at a time with the breath held. It cannot grade stenosis; digital subtraction angiography is the gold standard.
Digital subtraction angiography
Correct. Digital subtraction angiography is an invasive angiographic technique considered the gold standard; it is not used for screening but for guiding therapeutic interventions.
Duplex ultrasonography
Duplex ultrasonography is the most widely used initial screening and monitoring tool. The gold standard used to guide intervention is digital subtraction angiography.

set2.q: A 72-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation who takes no anticoagulant develops sudden, severe pain in her left leg two hours ago. The leg is cold and pale, pulses are absent below the femoral artery, and she has numbness over the dorsum of the foot. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Critical limb ischemia
Critical limb ischemia is chronic rest pain and tissue loss that builds over time. A sudden cold, pale, pulseless leg in atrial fibrillation is an acute embolic occlusion.
Atheroembolism with blue toes
Atheroemboli lodge in small vessels of skin and muscle, so distal pulses usually stay palpable. Absent pulses with a cold, pale leg point to an acute arterial occlusion.
Intermittent claudication
Claudication is predictable exertional pain relieved by rest. Abrupt pain at rest with a pulseless, cold leg is acute limb ischemia, a vascular emergency.
Acute embolic limb ischemia

Correct. Sudden occlusion of a previously patent artery with abrupt severe pain and absent pulses is acute limb ischemia; the heart is the embolic source in 80 to 90% of cases, atrial fibrillation being a classic example.

set2.q: A 64-year-old woman who smokes has cramping in her right calf after walking one block that eases after she stands still for several minutes. Her pedal pulses are diminished on the right. Which is the best initial test?
opts: Magnetic resonance angiography
Magnetic resonance angiography is an alternative for patients with contrast allergy when an intervention is planned. The initial study is the ankle-brachial index at the bedside.
Ankle-brachial index
Correct. The ankle-brachial index is a simple bedside test and the important initial test for suspected peripheral artery disease, comparing ankle to arm systolic pressure to grade severity.
Conventional angiography
Angiography is the invasive gold standard, used mainly to guide a planned intervention. It is not where the evaluation of new claudication begins; the ankle-brachial index is.
Computed tomography angiography
Computed tomography angiography needs contrast and is used mainly to plan an intervention. The first test for suspected disease is the bedside ankle-brachial index.

set2.q: A 66-year-old woman has had six days of worsening left leg pain and coolness. The limb has no sensory loss or weakness, and imaging shows an arterial thrombus. Which intervention fits this time frame?
opts: Catheter-directed thrombolysis
Correct. Intra-arterial catheter-directed thrombolysis, with alteplase as the thrombolytic, is indicated for acute limb ischemia of less than 14 days' duration.
Major amputation
Major amputation is reserved for irreversibly ischemic limbs with profound sensory loss and paralysis. Her viable limb within 14 days suits catheter-directed thrombolysis.
Oral aspirin alone
Aspirin is chronic antiplatelet therapy and will not dissolve an acute thrombus. Ischemia of under 14 days is an indication for catheter-directed thrombolysis.
Supervised exercise program
Exercise therapy is for chronic claudication. A new arterial thrombus under 14 days old is treated with catheter-directed thrombolysis.

set2.q: A 68-year-old man who smoked for 40 years has no symptoms, but a widened, pulsatile aorta is felt on routine abdominal examination. Which is the study of choice for initial screening for an aneurysm?
opts: Computed tomography angiography
Computed tomography angiography is the best diagnostic and pre-intervention planning study. The initial screening study for an aneurysm is abdominal ultrasound.
Magnetic resonance imaging
Magnetic resonance imaging is comparable to computed tomography without dye or radiation and suits stable patients with dye allergy. Screening starts with ultrasound.
Abdominal ultrasound
Correct. Abdominal ultrasound is the diagnostic study of choice for initial screening for the presence of an aneurysm and is also used for serial documentation of aneurysm size.
Abdominal X-ray
A plain film shows a calcified outline in only about 75% of aneurysms and misses the 25% that are not calcified. Ultrasound is the screening study of choice.

set2.q: A 71-year-old man has had progressive ischemic pain in his right leg for three weeks and is found to have an arterial occlusion. Which intervention falls outside its indication for him?
opts: Arterial bypass procedure
Arterial bypass is a listed surgical therapy for acute occlusion without a time limit. Catheter-directed thrombolysis is the option restricted to under 14 days.
Intravenous heparin
Anticoagulation with intravenous heparin is the medical therapy for acute occlusion. The intervention limited to under 14 days is catheter-directed thrombolysis.
Catheter-directed thrombolysis
Correct. Intra-arterial catheter-directed thrombolysis is indicated only for acute limb ischemia of less than 14 days' duration; at three weeks he is outside that window.
Surgical thromboembolectomy
Thromboembolectomy, by catheter or open surgery, is a listed therapy for acute peripheral arterial occlusion and carries no 14-day limit. Thrombolysis is the time-limited option.

set2.q: A 78-year-old man with no neurologic symptoms has a 90% carotid stenosis on duplex. He has advanced cancer, and his expected survival is about two years. Which management is most appropriate?
opts: Medical management

Correct. Surgery for an asymptomatic stenosis is advised only above 80% together with a life expectancy over five years. His limited survival means medical therapy: antiplatelets, risk-factor control and smoking cessation.
Carotid endarterectomy
The stenosis exceeds 80%, but asymptomatic surgery also requires a life expectancy of more than five years. With about two years, medical management is advised.
Carotid angioplasty with stenting
Stenting still counts as surgical revascularization and carries the same asymptomatic criteria, including life expectancy over five years. He should be managed medically.
Endarterectomy after one more duplex
Repeating the scan does not change the missing criterion, a life expectancy over five years. His asymptomatic stenosis is managed medically.

opts: Quit smoking; control blood pressure
Correct. Management of a thoracic aortic aneurysm includes smoking cessation, beta-adrenergic blockers and aggressive blood pressure control, with surveillance imaging for his size.
Blood pressure matters only after surgery
Aggressive blood pressure control is part of management now, before any surgery. Hypertension is common in patients with thoracic aneurysm.
Smoking matters only for leg disease
Smoking cessation is listed first in thoracic aneurysm management. Continuing to smoke works against him.
Nothing changes until repair
Medical management starts at diagnosis: stop smoking, beta blockade and aggressive blood pressure control, alongside surveillance.

set2.q: A 76-year-old man collapses with sudden severe back pain. He is pale, his blood pressure is 78/50, and a pulsatile abdominal mass is felt. There is a Grey Turner sign (flank ecchymosis). Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Large-bore access and emergency surgery
Correct. A ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm is hemodynamically unstable and a surgical emergency: large-bore intravenous catheters, type and crossmatch, and immediate operation.
Abdominal ultrasound surveillance
Surveillance ultrasound is for stable, asymptomatic aneurysms. Pain, a pulsatile mass and hypotension are the classic triad of rupture, a surgical emergency.
Admit for pain control and serial exams
Observation wastes time in a hemodynamically unstable rupture with retroperitoneal bleeding. Large-bore access and emergency surgery are needed.
Beta blocker, then elective repair
Beta blockers and planned repair suit a symptomatic but unruptured aneurysm. Hypotension with a flank bruise means rupture and a surgical emergency.

set2.q: A 65-year-old man has a painful, swollen right groin two days after a cardiac catheterization through the femoral artery. Ultrasound shows a blood-filled cavity outside the arterial wall, communicating with the lumen. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Femoral true aneurysm
A true aneurysm involves all three layers of the vessel wall. A cavity outside the wall after needle laceration is a false aneurysm, a pseudoaneurysm.
Acute limb ischemia
Acute limb ischemia is a sudden occlusion with a cold, pale, pulseless limb. A painful groin swelling with an extraluminal cavity is a pseudoaneurysm.
Atheroembolism
Atheroembolism causes painful blue toes with palpable pulses. A post-catheterization cavity outside the arterial wall is a pseudoaneurysm.
Femoral pseudoaneurysm

Correct. A pseudoaneurysm is a communication between the arterial lumen and overlying connective tissue after arterial rupture; the common site is the femoral artery after cardiac catheterization, from laceration by the access needle.

set2.q: A 74-year-old woman with known aortic atherosclerosis has sudden pain and tenderness of two toes, which have turned blue. Which pulse finding is expected on examination?
opts: A pulse with a double systolic peak
A double-peaked pulse is not a feature of limb emboli. With atheroembolism the expected finding is that distal pulses usually remain palpable.
Distal pulses usually remain palpable
Correct. Atheroembolic debris tends to lodge in small vessels of muscle and skin and may not occlude large vessels, so distal pulses usually remain palpable, unlike acute limb ischemia.
Pulses absent below the femoral artery
Absent pulses distal to an occlusion are the finding of acute limb ischemia from a thromboembolus. Small-vessel atheroemboli usually leave distal pulses palpable.
Pulses absent in both groins
Absent or diminished femoral pulses suggest aortoiliac disease, as in Leriche syndrome. Blue toes from atheroemboli usually come with palpable distal pulses.

opts: Screen with duplex every year
Serial duplex monitoring is for patients with known disease or after intervention. Routine screening of asymptomatic adults is recommended against.
Screen with angiography instead
Digital subtraction angiography is invasive and never used for screening; it guides interventions. Asymptomatic adults should not be screened at all.
Screen only if she smokes
Smoking raises stroke risk, but the recommendation is against screening the general asymptomatic adult population. Screening is not recommended for her.
Screening is not recommended

Correct. The preventive services task force recommended in 2014, and reaffirmed in 2021, against screening for asymptomatic carotid artery stenosis in the general adult population, as the harms of screening outweigh the benefits.

set2.q: A 73-year-old man with ischemic rest pain notices that walking around the room eases his foot pain, although walking used to cause calf pain. Which explanation should he be given?
opts: Walking releases natural pain relief
Rest pain is not relieved by a pain-relief response; it resists even narcotics. Standing and walking help because dependency lets gravity assist arterial flow.
Walking drains venous blood away
Venous drainage is not the reason. Standing and walking put the foot in a dependent position, and gravity then helps perfuse it.
Walking lowers his blood pressure
Lower pressure would reduce perfusion, not improve it. The relief comes from dependency, where gravity aids arterial flow to the forefoot.
Dependency uses gravity to aid flow
Correct. Rest pain is relieved by hanging the leg over the bed or walking around, a paradox: unlike claudication, walking uses the gravity effect of dependency on extremity perfusion.

set2.q: A 67-year-old woman with stable calf claudication is starting exercise therapy. She asks whether walking on her own at home is as good as a formal program. Which is the most appropriate recommendation?
opts: Refer to supervised exercise rehabilitation
Correct. Patients should be referred to an exercise rehabilitation program; a supervised program is more successful than a home-based one, and consistent moderate exercise improves walking distance.
Walk at home; supervision adds nothing
Home walking helps, but a supervised program is more successful than a home-based one. The recommendation is referral to supervised exercise rehabilitation.
Refer for bypass graft surgery now
Revascularization is for claudication with severe functional disability after an inadequate response to exercise or drugs. She has not yet had a trial of supervised exercise.
Avoid exercise until pain resolves
Waiting for pain to resolve before exercising delays the therapy that improves walking distance. Supervised exercise rehabilitation is the recommended referral.

set2.q: A 70-year-old man has claudication after half a block despite six months of supervised exercise, smoking cessation and cilostazol, and can no longer work. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Start intravenous heparin
Intravenous heparin is for acute limb ischemia, the sudden occlusion of a previously patent artery. Chronic disabling claudication after failed therapy calls for revascularization.
Proceed to amputation
Amputation is a last resort for nonviable limbs or failed revascularization. Disabling claudication without tissue loss first goes to revascularization.
Refer for revascularization

Correct. Revascularization is recommended for claudication with severe functional disability and an inadequate response to exercise or drug therapy, by endovascular angioplasty with or without stenting, atherectomy, or bypass.
Repeat the exercise program
He has already had an adequate supervised trial and remains severely disabled. The recommended escalation after failed exercise and drugs is revascularization.

set2.q: A 76-year-old woman has had painful blue toes for several days after atheroemboli from proximal plaques. Which complication may follow in the affected digits?
opts: Rupture of the popliteal artery
Atheroemboli block small digital vessels; they do not rupture large arteries. The complication in the toes is digital necrosis and gangrene.
Hoarseness from nerve stretch
Hoarseness comes from an aortic arch aneurysm stretching the recurrent laryngeal nerve. In the toes, atheroemboli can lead to digital necrosis and gangrene.
Heart block from nodal fibrosis
Nodal fibrosis is unrelated to limb emboli. Occluded digital vessels from atheroemboli can progress to digital necrosis and gangrene.
Digital necrosis and gangrene
Correct. Digital vascular occlusion from atheroemboli causes ischemia and blue toe syndrome, and digital necrosis and gangrene may develop in the affected toes.

set2.q: A 64-year-old woman has an asymptomatic ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm that now measures 5.9 cm. Repair is planned. Which approach is usually required for this location?
opts: Watch until it reaches 6.5 cm
The ascending threshold is 5.5 cm (6.0 cm is for descending). At 5.9 cm, repair is indicated, usually open with root replacement.
Open repair with root replacement
Correct. Surgery is generally indicated for ascending aneurysms over 5.5 cm, and an ascending aneurysm often requires an open surgical approach with aortic root replacement.
Endovascular repair only
Endovascular repair is an option for descending thoracic aneurysms. The ascending aorta usually needs open surgery with aortic root replacement.
Surveillance every 3 to 5 years
Three-to-five-yearly imaging is for aneurysms under 4.5 cm. At 5.9 cm in the ascending aorta she has passed the 5.5 cm threshold.

set2.q: A 71-year-old woman has sudden coolness of her left foot with minimal pain in the toes only. She has no sensory loss and no muscle weakness. Which prognosis applies to this limb?
opts: Salvageable if promptly treated
Correct. A marginally threatened limb, with minimal toe pain and no sensory loss or weakness, is salvageable if treated promptly, and there is time for vascular imaging first.
Not immediately threatened
A viable limb has no toe pain at all and is under no immediate threat. Minimal toe pain makes this limb marginally threatened: salvageable only if treated promptly.
Salvageable only with immediate revascularization
That prognosis belongs to the immediately threatened limb, with sensory loss beyond the toes and weakness. Her limb has neither, so prompt treatment suffices.
Major tissue loss is inevitable
Inevitable tissue loss or permanent nerve damage marks an irreversible limb with profound sensory loss and paralysis. This limb is still salvageable with prompt care.

set2.q: A 70-year-old woman has a 1.4 cm femoral pseudoaneurysm on ultrasound after cardiac catheterization. She is comfortable and the limb is well perfused. Which management is most appropriate?
opts: Catheter-directed thrombolysis
Thrombolysis dissolves clot in acute limb ischemia. A small pseudoaneurysm is expected to seal by clotting, so it is watched.
Watch and wait
Correct. A pseudoaneurysm under 2 cm in diameter may undergo spontaneous thrombosis and regression, so watchful waiting is appropriate.
Open surgical repair
Open surgery is not the listed treatment for a small pseudoaneurysm. Under 2 cm, it may thrombose and regress on its own with watchful waiting.
Intravenous heparin
Heparin anticoagulates and would work against the thrombosis that seals a pseudoaneurysm. Under 2 cm the plan is to watch and wait.

set2.q: A 67-year-old woman with hypertension has an acute aortic dissection with severe tearing chest pain and a blood pressure of 176/100. Which intravenous medication is appropriate to lower her pressure?
opts: Esmolol
Correct. Blood pressure in dissection is reduced with a beta blocker, esmolol being the named example, or a vasodilator such as nitroprusside, to a systolic of 100 to 120 mmHg.
Alteplase
Alteplase is the thrombolytic for catheter-directed treatment of acute limb ischemia. Dissection needs pressure reduction with esmolol or nitroprusside.
Heparin
Heparin anticoagulates acute limb ischemia. The dissection needs its blood pressure lowered, with esmolol or nitroprusside.
Cilostazol
Cilostazol is an oral antiplatelet for claudication. Acute dissection is treated by lowering pressure with esmolol or nitroprusside.

set2.q: A 68-year-old man had a transient ischemic attack last month. Duplex shows 85% stenosis of the ipsilateral internal carotid artery, and he is a good surgical candidate. Which treatment is most appropriate?
opts: Antiplatelet therapy alone
Medical management alone is advised for low-grade stenosis under 50%. A symptomatic 85% stenosis meets the threshold for surgical intervention.
Carotid stenting via the groin
Carotid angioplasty with stenting is less invasive and suits poor surgical candidates. In a good surgical candidate, endarterectomy is the gold standard.
Repeat duplex in one year
Serial duplex monitoring suits disease below the surgical threshold. A symptomatic 85% stenosis needs revascularization, with endarterectomy as the gold standard.
Carotid endarterectomy

Correct. Surgery is advised for symptomatic patients with more than 70% stenosis, and carotid endarterectomy, removal of plaque through a surgical incision, is the gold standard for high-grade carotid stenosis.

set2.q: A 66-year-old man is newly diagnosed with peripheral artery disease after an abnormal ankle-brachial index. He has no chest symptoms. Because half of such patients share it, which associated condition should be evaluated next?
opts: Pseudoaneurysm of the femoral artery
A femoral pseudoaneurysm follows arterial puncture during catheterization. The condition shared by half of patients with peripheral artery disease is coronary artery disease.
Venous insufficiency
Venous insufficiency is a differential for leg pain, not a coexisting disease in half of these patients. Coronary artery disease is present in 50% of them.
Coronary artery disease
Correct. Peripheral artery disease shares the pathophysiology of coronary artery disease, and 50% of patients with peripheral artery disease also have coronary artery disease, so it should be sought.
Aortic dissection
Aortic dissection presents with sudden tearing chest pain and is not a condition half of these patients carry. The association to evaluate is coronary artery disease.

set2.q: A 71-year-old man's asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm measured 4.1 cm six months ago and now measures 4.8 cm. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Wait until it reaches 5.5 cm
Size is only one trigger; rapid expansion of 0.5 cm in six months is another. His 0.7 cm growth means repair now, not waiting.
Repair the aneurysm
Correct. Evidence of rapid growth, 0.5 cm in six months, is an indication for repair regardless of size; his aneurysm grew 0.7 cm, and fast expansion also raises rupture risk.
Ultrasound in three years
Three-yearly surveillance is for stable 3.0 to 3.9 cm aneurysms. Growth of 0.7 cm in six months is rapid and calls for repair.
Recheck in 6 to 12 months
That interval is for a stable 4.0 to 5.4 cm aneurysm. Rapid growth of more than 0.5 cm in six months is itself an indication for repair.

set2.q: A 72-year-old man has an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm measuring 4.2 cm, unchanged from last year. Which follow-up is most appropriate?
opts: Elective repair now
At 4.2 cm and not growing, he is below every repair threshold (5.0 cm women, over 5.5 cm men, or 0.5 cm growth in six months). Surveillance continues.
Emergency repair today
Emergency surgery is for a ruptured aneurysm with pain, a pulsatile mass and hypotension. An asymptomatic, stable 4.2 cm aneurysm is surveyed every six to 12 months.
Imaging every 6 to 12 months
Correct. Surveillance frequency depends on size: an aneurysm of 4.0 to 5.4 cm is imaged with ultrasound or computed tomography every six to 12 months.
Ultrasound every three years
Three-yearly ultrasound is for aneurysms of 3.0 to 3.9 cm. At 4.2 cm the interval shortens to every six to 12 months.

set2.q: A 70-year-old man with a 6.1 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm is scheduled for elective repair. He asks how the surgeon will choose between endovascular and open repair. Which factor guides the choice?
opts: His age and comorbidities

Correct. Two methods exist, endovascular aneurysm repair with a modular graft placed through the iliac or femoral arteries, and open replacement with a tube or bifurcated graft; the choice considers age and medical comorbidities.
The color of his skin
Skin color has no bearing on the repair method. The surgeon weighs the patient's age and medical comorbidities in choosing endovascular or open repair.
The result of his ankle index
The ankle-brachial index grades leg arterial disease and does not choose the aneurysm repair. Age and comorbidities decide between endovascular and open.
Whether he has a carotid bruit
A carotid bruit relates to carotid disease, not the aortic repair method. The choice between endovascular and open repair rests on age and comorbidities.

set2.q: A 72-year-old man is diagnosed with an acute aortic dissection. His family asks what happens if it is not treated. Which statement is accurate?
opts: Only the legs are at risk
Dissection is an intimal tear of the aorta itself, with syncope, blood pressure swings and aortic regurgitation. Untreated, mortality is high.
Untreated, mortality is high
Correct. Acute untreated aortic dissection carries a high mortality rate, which is why blood pressure is lowered at once, pain is controlled and surgical grafting of the diseased aorta is pursued.
It usually heals by itself
Nothing supports spontaneous healing as the expected course. Acute untreated dissection has a high mortality rate.
It turns into a pseudoaneurysm
A pseudoaneurysm is a separate lesion from arterial puncture. The danger of untreated acute dissection is a high mortality rate.

set2.q: A 64-year-old man with long-standing hypertension has sudden, severe, tearing chest pain radiating to his back. Blood pressure is 184/106. Imaging confirms an aortic dissection. Which blood pressure goal applies first?
opts: Systolic above 140 mmHg
Keeping systolic pressure above 140 mmHg leaves the dissection free to propagate. The goal is to lower it to 100 to 120 mmHg.
Systolic below 80 mmHg
Driving pressure below 80 mmHg risks shock and organ hypoperfusion. The goal is systolic 100 to 120 mmHg.
No change until surgery
Waiting for surgery without lowering pressure allows the tear to extend. Pressure reduction to systolic 100 to 120 mmHg comes first.
Systolic 100 to 120 mmHg
Correct. Management stops progression by reducing blood pressure, bringing systolic pressure to 100 to 120 mmHg with a beta blocker such as esmolol or a vasodilator such as nitroprusside.

Repair the aneurysm

Six-to-12-monthly imaging is surveillance for an asymptomatic 4.5 to 5.4 cm aneurysm. Once it causes symptoms, repair is recommended.
Imaging every 3 to 5 years

set2.q: A 66-year-old man has lifestyle-limiting calf claudication despite six months of supervised exercise and antiplatelet therapy, and revascularization is being planned. Which study is the gold standard for defining his arterial anatomy?
opts: Ankle-brachial index
The ankle-brachial index is the simple bedside initial test that grades severity. It cannot map arterial anatomy for revascularization; conventional angiography does.
Pulse volume recording
Pulse volume recordings in the vascular laboratory localize the site and severity of disease. The gold standard for anatomy before an intervention is conventional angiography.
Conventional angiography

Correct. Conventional angiography is the gold standard, the most accurate and informative test. It is invasive, requiring vascular puncture and contrast at the stenosis, and is used mainly to guide a planned intervention.
Duplex ultrasound
Duplex ultrasound is the mainstay initial noninvasive imaging for suspected stenosis. It needs no contrast or radiation, but it is not the gold standard; conventional angiography is.

opts: Kidney stones and gout flares
Stones and gout are unrelated to arterial bypass. He should hear about myocardial infarction, stroke, graft infection and peripheral embolization.
Heart attack, stroke, graft infection
Correct. Bypass graft surgery is highly effective, but its complications include myocardial infarction and stroke, infection of the graft, and peripheral embolization.
Hoarseness and difficulty swallowing
Hoarseness and dysphagia are compression symptoms of thoracic aortic aneurysms of the arch and descending aorta. Bypass risks are infarction, stroke, graft infection and embolization.
Heart block needing a pacemaker
